edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1      1 (same on all six pages, page number at right, no id)
edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page.

For K-1, say 'Use the regular blocks, not the big ones.' A kindergartner who hears 'small blocks' may think only green triangles are allowed, which clashes with Problem 4's palette of hexagon, trapezoid and chevron.

k-1.summary: Six actual-size problems give K-1 real ideas with the blocks: possible and impossible shapes (including an even-area trapezoid that still fails), fewest greens on triangles of side 2-4 (2, 3, 4), all coverings of two small hexagons (2 and 3), fewest blocks with the full set (3, 3, 4), a placement game (answers 1, 2, 1, 1, 2), and the six coverings of a 2-1-2 hexagon. I checked every answer and all are correct; the only edits are the footer and one wording fix. The problems are more a sampler of separate ideas than one developed thread, and for kindergartners 'can always win' and Problem 6 will need the adult.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1      1 (same on all seven pages, page number at right, no id)
edits.fix: Use the standard footer 'Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1 / <id>' on every page.

edits.quote: Imagine a triangle board with 10 small triangles along each side. ... What if the board has 100 small triangles along each side?
edits.fix: The bottom row of a side-n triangle holds 2n-1 small triangles, so children who count triangles in the row will get the wrong size. Name the size by edges instead: 'a triangle board whose sides are each 10 small-triangle edges long' (and the same for 100).

edits.quote: 2 small triangles on each side / 3 small triangles on each side / 4 small triangles on each side / 5 small triangles on each side
edits.fix: Label the table rows to match the corrected wording in P4 (for example 'side 2', 'side 3', ...), or refer to the Problem 3 triangles by size from smallest to largest.

grades-2-3.summary: This band develops the coloring obstruction step by step through contrasting boards. P1 has an odd-area board, an even but unbalanced board, a forced star tiling and a hexagon. P2 adds the bowtie F, whose up and down counts balance but whose halves touch only at a point, and the holes in E (two ups, impossible) against G (one up and one down, 4 coverings). After that come fewest greens with a proof, the general case for sides 10 and 100, chevrons against rhombuses (4, 5, 4, 5 against 2, 3, 4, 5), a board-design task that can be solved (for example a 13-up, 7-down comb), and a two-hole rule; I checked by computer that every up/down pair of holes works. Only wording edits remain, and the main limit on level is how much written explanation third graders are asked for.

edits.quote: Bellingham Math Circle / Week 1      1 (same on all eight pages, page number at right, no id)

edits.quote: On the hexagon board each covering has two ribbons, because its top side has two short edges.
edits.fix: The Problem 1 board is also a hexagon, so name the board: 'On the board from Problem 3, each covering has two ribbons.' Cut the 'because' clause, which only restates the definition.

edits.quote: Explain why, whenever you make flips on the hexagon board ... Then find the smallest number of flips that changes covering E into covering F in Problem 3, and explain why nobody can do it with fewer.
edits.fix: Problem 3 already asks for the smallest number of flips from E to F (the answer is 8), so children will wonder whether to redo it. Rewrite as: 'Explain why nobody can change covering E into covering F with fewer flips than your answer in Problem 3.' Also change 'the hexagon board' to 'the board from Problem 3'.

grades-4-5.summary: This band follows kernel 2 closely: all six coverings of the 1-2-2 hexagon (with 10 recording boards, so the count is not given away), the flip graph, and flip-distance puzzles with answers A to B 3, C to D 4 and E to F 8, which I read from the drawings and checked by computer. It goes on to 4-flip round trips from A (they exist, and 5 or 7 flips are impossible), ribbons with a correct worked LRRLR example, the parity proof, and counting 20 coverings two ways (side-2 hexagon and 1-3-3 hexagon). There is well over forty minutes of substantial work. The edits are a duplicated question and an ambiguous board name in P5 and P6, plus the footer.

overall.strongest: Grades 2-3 builds the coloring obstruction through well-chosen contrasting boards (E vs G holes, the bowtie F, triangles of side 2-5) and ends in real generalization, invention and rule-finding, all of it mathematically correct.
overall.weakest: K-1 is correct and substantial but reads as a sampler of separate tasks (impossibility, fewest greens, all coverings, fewest blocks, a game) rather than one developed idea, and its strategy question and six-covering hexagon will lean heavily on the adult for kindergartners.
